items.heading: Talk to One Person Actually
items.text: Talk to One Person Actually Talk to one person actually doing the job or holding the seat, and ask what a normal week looks like and what they wish they had known.

items.heading: Pick Two Lanes and Give
items.text: Pick Two Lanes and Give Pick Two Lanes and Give Pick two lanes and give each a real trial: apply to a few entry-level roles for one, and sit one full past paper under exam conditions for the other. Score it honestly.

items.heading: This Lane Pays Soonest
items.text: This lane pays soonest and lets you learn on someone else's budget. It works best when you treat the first job as paid training with a plan, not as a place to sit.

rows: Work now, add skills on the job
A visible skill on top of the BA, and the nerve to apply before you feel ready.
Soonest. Offers can start within weeks of a solid portfolio.
Entry pay is modest. Without a second skill you can sit at the same salary for years.
Study one more degree (MA, MBA, LLB, B.Ed, PG diploma)
Fees, one to three more years, and an entrance exam for most good seats.
Delayed by the length of the course.
A second degree only pays if the seat, the institute and the placement record justify the fee.
Competitive exam (UPSC, SSC, banking, teaching eligibility)
Long, focused preparation and the ability to absorb a real chance of no result.
Unpredictable. Years for some, never for most.
Very high stability if you get in, very low odds per attempt. You need a parallel plan.

visuals.heading: Build One Small Proof Piece

items.heading: Build One Small Proof Piece
items.text: Build one small proof piece for the lane you lean towards and show it to two people who could hire or advise you. When you message them, keep it to one specific observation about their work, a link to your proof, and one small question.

items.heading: Decide with What You Learned
items.text: Decide with what you learned. Some people know within a few weeks; others need a couple of months of real exposure. Both are normal.

visuals.heading: Take Your Family's Total Education

items.heading: Take Your Family's Total Education
items.text: Take your family's total education and security budget. Treat about 10% for the college as a strict starting benchmark, not a law.

items.heading: Spending Above Roughly 20% Needs
items.text: Spending above roughly 20% needs course-specific proof: placement median, licence requirement, faculty and alumni access.

items.heading: Keep the Rest for Living
items.text: Keep the rest for living costs, tools, internet, projects and upskilling after the degree.
